NYC ballot · Nov 3, 2026 · Unofficial election night results

Prop 3 support vs. the protected bike network

New York City passed Proposal 3, a charter amendment to speed up street safety projects, on Nov 3, 2026. This map compares support in each of the city's ~4,000 election districts with the protected bike lanes nearby and the share of households without a car, to show where support outruns the infrastructure.

This page was built with Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. The data processing, analysis and code were AI-generated under human direction. Figures come from the public sources listed in Acknowledgements; check them against those sources before citing.

Protected/greenway · painted · shared

Bike scoring

How each precinct's bike infrastructure score is built, from the NYC DOT bike route file (current segments only).

Method

  1. Rate each side of the street. Every segment lists a facility for each direction of travel. Each direction gets the weight in the table, and the segment's weight is the average of the two. A two-way protected path scores 1.0 per km; a one-way protected lane scores 0.5.
  2. Draw a 0.5 km circle around each precinct. That's roughly a five-minute walk or two-minute ride. The tight radius rewards a dense network: a precinct only scores well if protected routes run close by, not somewhere in the wider neighborhood.
  3. Add up weighted kilometers of every segment inside the circle. The result is the precinct's score, in quality-weighted km.

What's left out

  • Shared lanes, sharrows, signed routes and wide parking lanes score zero. Riders share them with cars.
  • Painted lanes count for 5–10% of a protected lane, because nothing separates them from traffic.
  • Retired segments and exact duplicate geometries are dropped.
  • The DOT file doesn't say what kind of protection a lane has, so concrete barriers, parked cars and plastic posts all count as "Protected."
  • Greenways and on-street protected lanes are weighted the same.

Weights and what they add up to

FacilityWeightRoute kmShare of score

Route km counts each direction as half a route, so a two-way facility counts once. Share of score is each facility's share of the weighted total across the whole city. Protected facilities drive almost all of it.

Reading the support gap

Both measures are ranked across 3,920 precincts with at least 50 votes.

The gap is a precinct's Yes-share percentile minus its bike-score percentile. Purple means support ranks higher than the bike network around it; blue means the bike network ranks higher than the support. The two rankings are only loosely related (rank correlation 0.25). Proposal 3 also covered city property and office leasing, and some voters say Yes to ballot questions by habit, so Yes share is an imperfect stand-in for demand for bike lanes.

Support most ahead of infrastructure

    Infrastructure most ahead of support

      Assembly Districts, vote-weighted average gap. Neighborhood names are approximate.

      Opportunity

      Support gap × share of households without a car: where support outruns the bike network and most households don't drive.

      This layer weights the gap by how many households depend on something other than a car. A precinct whose Yes share ranks 40 points above its bike score, where 75% of households don't own a car, scores 40 × 0.75 = 30. Precincts where the bike network ranks at or above support have no shortfall and are shown flat; higher scores mean strong support, little protected infrastructure and many car-free households.

      Highest-scoring Assembly Districts

        Vote-weighted average score across each district's precincts, then car-free share and number of precincts scoring 30 or more.

        How to read it

        • Both inputs are relative. The gap compares precincts' rankings, so a high score means "underbuilt compared with the rest of the city," not an absolute shortage.
        • Car-free share is a five-year survey estimate spread from census tracts, so single-precinct values are approximate; clusters are more meaningful than individual precincts.
        • Yes share stands in for demand, but Proposal 3 also covered city property and office leasing.

        Car ownership and support

        Share of households with no vehicle available, American Community Survey 2017–2021 five-year estimates, by census tract.

        Car-free households track support more closely than anything else on this page. Yes share rises steadily with the share of households that don't own a car, and car ownership tracks Yes share (rank correlation 0.48) much more closely than the bike network does (0.25). The bike network itself follows car ownership (0.57): protected lanes are concentrated where fewer people drive.

        Households without a carPrecinctsYes share

        Tract estimates are spread onto precincts by area, so a precinct's figure reflects its surrounding tracts and carries the survey's margin of error. Precincts with fewer than 20 estimated households are left blank.

        Acknowledgements

        This map is built entirely from public data. Thanks to the agencies and people who publish it. None of them produced or endorsed this analysis.

        Election results
        NYC Board of Elections, unofficial election night results for Proposal 3, Nov 3, 2026 (as of Nov 4, 12:42 AM), by Assembly District and election district. Totals will change as remaining ballots are counted; certified results come later.
        Election district boundaries
        NYC Department of City Planning, Election Districts, release 25C, from its Political and Administrative Districts data. The copy used here comes from the public ry-li/map-nyc-election repository on GitHub.
        Bike routes
        NYC Department of Transportation, New York City Bike Routes, published through NYC Open Data. Current segments only. The quality weights, 0.5 km radius, gap and opportunity scores are this project's own (see Bike scoring and Opportunity).
        Car ownership
        U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2017–2021 five-year estimates (vehicles available by household), as processed for 2020 census tracts by the NYC Department of City Planning for Population FactFinder, including DCP's 2010–2020 tract crosswalk.
        Census tract boundaries
        NYC Department of City Planning, 2010 Census Tracts (release 20A), from the NYC Health Department's public nycehs/NYC_geography repository. Car ownership was mapped onto these tracts with the crosswalk, then spread onto precincts by area.
        Inspiration
        The CUNY Graduate Center's Center for Urban Research, whose NYC 2026 election map was the starting point for this project.
        Typefaces and tools
        Source Serif 4, Public Sans and IBM Plex Mono via Google Fonts. Data processed in Python with shapely, pyproj, pyshp and openpyxl. Analysis and map built with the help of Claude, an AI model by Anthropic.
        Data notes: results are unofficial, with 81–99% of scanners reported by Assembly District. Precinct results sum exactly to the official Assembly District and citywide totals. 8 precincts redrawn for 2026 (3,064 votes, 0.2% of the total) have no boundary in the 25C release and are left off the map. Small cross-borough fragments (AD 37 in Manhattan with 0 votes, AD 61 in Brooklyn with 2) are folded into their main district.
